_comment: Hindu expansion 175-drive C: Upanishad story-episodes (Müller SBE 1879/1884, public domain). Classified 'religious' (canonical scripture).

title.en: The Two Birds on the One Tree

region.zh: 阿闥婆學派（象徵性定位於迦屍）

texts.period: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1, late Vedic, c. 6th-2nd c. BCE (Müller translation, 1884)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 15)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part II, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 15, 1884), Mundaka Upanishad, Mundaka III, Khanda 1

summary.en: Two birds, fast friends, perch on the same tree: one eats the tree's sweet and bitter fruit, the other looks on without eating. When the eater, sunk in grief at his impotence, sees that other, his grief melts - and he knows it is he. The tree is the world, the birds are the self and the Self.
summary.zh: 雙鳥為友，同棲一樹：一隻啄食樹上的甘果與苦果，另一隻不食而觀。食果者陷於自力無能之悲，一旦望見那一位，悲即消融——他知那也是他自己。樹即世界，雙鳥即自我與大我。

passages.text: Two birds, fast bound in friendship, sit on the same tree; one of them eats the sweet fig, the other, not eating, looks on. On the same tree the person sits, sunk and grieving, bewildered; but when he sees the other, the Lord, contented, and knows his glory, then his grief passes away from him. The knowing bird crosses: he becomes free, immortal, and light is shed on the tree's whole meaning - the image behind the later Sufi and Christian birds-on-a-branch alike, carried from the same Vedic source.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.1 (Müller 1884); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.2 (Müller 1884); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.3 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Satyakama Jabala: The Boy Who Told the Truth
title.zh: 薩底耶迦摩：說真話的男孩

texts.period: Chandogya Upanishad 4.4-9, c. 8th-6th c. BCE (Müller translation, 1879)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part I, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 1, 1879), Chandogya Upanishad, Prapathaka IV

summary.en: The boy Satyakama wants to study, but has no father's name to claim. His mother Jabala tells him to say exactly what she told him - and the teacher Haridrumata accepts him because he did not swerve from truth. Sent to tend four hundred cows, he is taught the knowledge of Brahman one element at a time by a bull, fire, a swan and a diver-bird.
summary.zh: 男孩薩底耶迦摩欲求學，卻無父名可報。母親闍波羅囑其如實轉述；師哈里陀魯摩多因其不離真語而收之。遣其牧牛四百，牛、火、天鵝與潛水鳥逐一為其教授梵之知識，一次一種元素。

passages.text: Satyakama, asking to be taught, named himself by his mother alone; asked what family he was of, he said: I have asked my mother, and she said she served many men in her youth, so she does not know - I am Satyakama Jabala, and I will tell you what she told me.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 4.4 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

passages.text: The teacher answered: none but a Brahmin would speak so; fetch the fuel, my boy, I shall not let you swerve from truth - and he gave him four hundred cows to keep until they were a thousand, and told him not to come back until then.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 4.4 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the forest, teachers of unlikely species came: the bull taught him one quarter of Brahman (light), the fire another (the quarters and the world), the swan the third (light through the eye), the diver-bird the fourth (the Person in the eye) - and Satyakama came home with a face of peace and knew the whole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 4.5-9 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

title.en: Indra Studies the Self for a Hundred and One Years
title.zh: 因陀羅求學自我一百零一年

region.zh: 生主天界（象徵性定位於俱盧之野）

texts.period: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7-12, c. 8th-6th c. BCE (Müller translation, 1879)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part I, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 1, 1879), Chandogya Upanishad, Prapathaka VIII

summary.en: The gods and demons both want the Self that is 'free from evil, old age, death, sorrow, hunger, thirst'. Prajapati teaches first Virochana the demon ('the Self is the body' - who goes home rich in that error) and then Indra the god, who tests three answers - the dreaming self, the sleeping self, the self in deep sleep - and is told each time that it is not this. Only after thirty-two more years of study does the doctrine of the body-transcending Self arrive.
summary.zh: 神與魔都想得到『離惡、老、死、憂、飢、渴』之自我。生主先教惡魔毗羅折那『自我即身體』——其人滿載此誤而歸——再教神因陀羅；因陀羅試驗三種答案——夢中之我、酣睡之我、深眠之我——每次皆被告知『非此』。再經三十二年苦學，超越身體的自我之教方至。

passages.text: Prajapati's syllabus is the premise: seek the Self that is free from evil, free from old age, death and sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are real and whose thoughts are true - that is the self that should be sought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 8.7 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

passages.text: The demon's short course: look at yourself in a pan of water, in a mirror - that well-adorned self is the Self; body is Self, and there is no other world. Virochana went home and taught his demons: the body is the self, serve the body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 8.8 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

passages.text: Indra saw the flaw at once - a body is stripped, blind, dumb by injury, so the body-self dies too - and stayed on for the second and third lessons (the dream-self, the deep-sleep-self), each refuted, until, after a hundred and one years of study, Prajapati taught him the Self beyond the body: the light beyond darkness, the self that goes where it wills - and Indra, satisfied, knew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 8.9-12 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

title.en: The Yaksha and Uma: Who Is the Breath Behind the Deeds?
title.zh: 夜叉與塢摩：行為背後的氣息是誰？

region.zh: 塢摩之喜馬拉雅居所（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kena Upanishad 3-4, late Vedic, c. 5th-2nd c. BCE (Müller translation, 1884)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 15)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part II, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 15, 1884), Kena (Talavakara) Upanishad, Khanda III-IV

summary.en: Brahman won a great victory for the gods - but the gods did not know who had really won it. A shining being appeared before them; Agni could not burn a straw before it, Vayu could not lift it; Indra approached - and the being vanished, replaced by Uma, the daughter of the mountains, who revealed: 'It is Brahman; in that victory you exult.' The gods won nothing of themselves.
summary.zh: 梵為諸神贏得一場大勝——但諸神不知真正獲勝者是誰。一道閃耀者現於其前；阿耆尼不能於其前燃草，伐由不能舉之；因陀羅近前——此存在消隱，代之以塢摩，山之女，揭示道：『那是梵；你們所誇的勝利屬於祂。』諸神自身一無所獲。

passages.text: Brahman gained a victory for the gods, and the gods exulted - 'ours is the victory' - but Brahman knew their thought, and a great Yaksha appeared before them, unknown and bright. Agni was sent to see what spirit it was; he could approach but not burn a blade of grass set before it, and returned owning defeat; Vayu the wind could not move a straw before it; then Indra drew near, and the being vanished from before his eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kena Upanishad 3.1-2 (Müller 1884); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Kena Upanishad 3.3-8 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: In that very region Indra saw Uma, Haimavati, the daughter of the snow mountains, shining, and asked her who the great Yaksha was; she answered: it is Brahman - in that victory you exult, and it was his. Therefore the gods excel the demons, for they came to know it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kena Upanishad 4.1-3 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Rudra the One God of the Many Faces

region.zh: 白騾仙人居所（象徵性定位於俱盧之野）

texts.period: Svetasvatara Upanishad 3-4, late Vedic, c. 5th-2nd c. BCE (Müller translation, 1884)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 15)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part II, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 15, 1884), Svetasvatara Upanishad, Adhyaya III-IV

summary.en: The Svetasvatara is the Upanishads' theistic hymn: Rudra, the fire-faced, gold-limbed god of a thousand heads, is proclaimed the one Lord behind all the fires, all the suns, all the waters - and, more dangerous still, behind the very notion of many gods: 'he is the one god hidden in all beings; he who knows him becomes immortal'.
summary.zh: 《白騾奧義書》是奧義書中的有神頌：樓陀羅，火面金肢、千首之神，被宣告為一切火、一切日、一切水背後的唯一之主——更險的是：在『多神』觀念的背後——『彼為藏於萬有之中的一神；知彼者得不死』。

passages.text: The One is without parts, without activities, calm, faultless, taintless, like a fire that has consumed its fuel - immortal, the bridge of the fearless; the hymn then names the bridge: Rudra. That one god, hidden in all beings, not shining forth, is to be sought; the many gods are his faces - fire his head, sun and moon his eyes, sky his body, earth his feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Svetasvatara Upanishad 3.15, 3.20 (Müller 1884); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Svetasvatara Upanishad 3.11, 4.2-3 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old rivalry is rewritten: Rudra is said to be the one god in the waters, in the fire, in the whole world, in plants and herbs - and the tradition's later Shiva-language ('lord of the lords, than whom there is none greater') is already sounding here.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Svetasvatara Upanishad 4.10-12 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Yajnavalkya and Maitreyi: Not Through Wealth Is Immortality
title.zh: 祭皮衣那與彌特勒耶：不朽不因財富

region.en: Videha, Janaka's court (symbolic pin at Mithila)
region.zh: 韋提訶，遮那迦王廷（象徵性定位於彌提羅）

texts.period: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4, c. 8th-6th c. BCE (Müller translation, 1884)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 15)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part II, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 15, 1884), Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Adhyaya II, Brahmana 4

summary.en: About to renounce the world, Yajnavalkya offers to divide his property between his two wives. Maitreyi asks whether wealth can make her immortal - 'no', says the sage, 'like the life of the rich will be the life of those who possess wealth' - and asks instead for the teaching. What he gives her is the doctrine of the Self as the dearest of all things, and a famous picture of grief: where there is duality, one sees another; where there is nothing but the Self, who sees whom?
summary.zh: 祭皮衣那將出家，欲把財產分與二妻。彌特勒耶問財富能否使其不朽——『不能』，仙人答——『有財者之命，如富人之命』——轉而求教。所授者即自我為萬物中最親者的教義，以及一張著名的悲傷圖：有二者之處，一者見另一者；唯自我獨存之處，誰見誰？

passages.text: Maitreyi said: if all this earth filled with wealth were mine, would it make me immortal? No, said Yajnavalkya, like the life of the rich would be thy life; but there is no hope of immortality by wealth. Then, said she, what should I do with that by which I cannot become immortal? - teach me.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.2-3 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The teaching is about love and dearness: not for the husband's sake is the husband dear, but for the sake of the Self; not for the wife's sake is the wife dear - all things are dear for the sake of the Self in them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the grief-picture: where there is anything like duality, one sees another, one smells another, one knows another - but when all has become the Self only, who is seen by whom, who is known by whom? This is the great, unborn Self, the giver of all bliss - and Maitreyi, hearing, was satisfied.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.12-14 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Six Questions of the Sages

region.zh: 畢疊利陀仙人道場（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Prashna Upanishad, late Vedic, c. 5th-2nd c. BCE (Müller translation, 1884)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 15)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part II, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 15, 1884), Prashna Upanishad

summary.en: Six students come to the sage Pippalada and are told: live with me a year in austerity, faith and self-restraint, then ask what you wish. Their year's discipline completed, they ask the six questions of the Prashna - whence are creatures born, what lord dwells in the body, whence comes this breath, what is waking and sleep, what fruits meditation, and what is the Person of sixteen parts - and each is answered.
summary.zh: 六位學子來到仙人畢疊利陀之處，被告知：以苦行、信與自制與我同住一年，然後任問所欲。一年修行畢，他們提出《六問》——眾生何由而生？何主居於身中？此息何從而來？何為醒與眠？靜觀結何果？十六分之人是什麼？——一一得答。

passages.text: Six seekers came with fuel in hand - the gesture of the brahmacharin asking for study - and Pippalada told them to stay with him a year in faith and austerity before asking; they kept the year. The answers map a body-cosmos: the breath is the axle on which everything turns; in sleep the mind gathers its light into the breath; in waking the senses go out; and above both is the Person - the sixteen parts returning one by one to their source like rivers to the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Prashna Upanishad 1.1-2 (Müller 1884); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Prashna Upanishad 3-6 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The final question - who is the person of sixteen parts - is answered with a cosmogony from the letter Om to the elements, and the students' blessing ends the book: thou art our father, who takest us across to the other shore of ignorance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Prashna Upanishad 6 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lord Settled in All Things

region.en: White Yajus school (symbolic pin at Kashi)
region.zh: 白夜柔學派（象徵性定位於迦屍）

texts.period: Isha Upanishad, late Vedic, c. 5th-2nd c. BCE (Müller translation, 1884)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 15)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part II, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 15, 1884), Isa Upanishad

summary.en: The Isha Upanishad is eighteen verses of compressed ethics: the Lord dwells in all moving and unmoving things - 'enjoy by renouncing, covet not' - and the self in all beings is to be seen as oneself, grief and delusion dissolving there. Its last verses send the dying person's light toward the sun, the oldest prayer for a good death.
summary.zh: 《自在奧義書》為十八節壓縮的倫理學：主遍在動與不動的一切——『以捨而享，勿起貪求』——萬有中的自我當被視作自我，悲與妄於彼消融。末節送垂死者之光向日，是為善終的最古老祈禱。

passages.text: All this, whatsoever moves in this moving world, is inhabited by the Lord; enjoy it by renouncing it - do not covet any man's wealth. He who sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, never turns away from it; for him, seeing all beings as his own self, there is no delusion and no grief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Isha Upanishad 1 (Müller 1884); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Isha Upanishad 6-7 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The final verses are for the dying face: the golden face of the sun is covered with a golden dish - remove it, that the doer of truth may look on light; let my breath reach the immortal breath; remember what I have done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Isha Upanishad 15-17 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.
